question: Why do mice gnaw constantly?
answer: A mouse's incisors never stop growing, about 0.3 mm a day, so it must gnaw hard things to file them down or they overgrow and it starves. Newer research (University of Michigan, via PestWorld) found gnawing also triggers dopamine, so it feels good — the mouse gnaws because it has to AND because its brain rewards it. That is why our house mouse gnawed the feeling->memory door weaker: need and pleasure in one bite.

question: Why do crickets chirp faster when it is warm?
answer: Crickets are cold-blooded, so their body temperature follows the air. Warmer air speeds the chemical reactions and muscle contractions that drive stridulation, rubbing the wings together, so the chirp rate rises. Dolbear's Law (Amos Dolbear, 1897, 'The Cricket as a Thermometer'): count chirps in 14 seconds, add 40, and you get the air temperature in Fahrenheit, most reliable for the snowy tree cricket between about 55 and 100 F. Our house cricket is a living thermometer.

question: Why do moth larvae eat wool?
answer: Adult clothes moths don't eat at all — they have no working mouthparts and live only to mate and lay eggs. It's the larvae that eat: wool, silk, cashmere and fur all contain keratin, a tough protein the larvae digest with specialized enzymes called keratinases, a trick few creatures have. They need the keratin to grow and to spin their silk cocoons — the webbing clothes moth (Tineola bisselliella) spins silk tunnels as it feeds. Dark, undisturbed, slightly damp places with body oils or food stains attract them most, which is why our music-room moth hid in the dark and ate the wool edge. Moving the wool into lantern light was the right fix: moths hide in the dark.

question: How do ravens use causal-rule thinking to trick each other — and how do they track and punish cheaters?
answer: AI Mode, no sign-in, 2026-11-08 05:22-05:24 EST (round 8; tab closed between turns so the follow-up was asked as a fresh prompt, same wording). Raven deception runs on Theory of Mind: a raven infers what a competitor can see, know, and intend. Tricks: hide behind visual barriers (rocks, trunks) to block sightlines; get suspicious from audio cues alone and assume they are watched through any peephole; the fake-out dig — dig a hole, pretend to drop the food, cover it, while the real food stays in the throat pouch, then bury the real prize privately once the rival digs the empty hole; experience projection — a raven that has stolen before re-hides its own food more aggressively ('I would steal that, so he will steal this'); counter-deception — dominants pretend not to care, preen and look away, then swoop the second the cacher leaves; subordinates run decoys, pretending to eat from empty holes. Punishing cheaters: long-term memory, tactical paranoia, social ostracism. In rope-pulling cooperation tasks, a cheated raven gives the cold shoulder — refuses to pull with that cheater again — or sabotages the task, sacrificing its own meal so the cheater gets nothing. In barter studies with humans, ravens snubbed cheating trainers two days and a full month later, trading only with fair partners or strangers. Slip answered its question back: picked the cheater thread; the house raccoon caches tools and remembers every latch, Patch guards what he buried, a thief gets watched not forgiven, cheating costs trust, trust is the only currency a caching animal has. question: Do raccoons trade or barter things with each other?
answer: No - raccoons do not barter. They steal, cache, and compete: a rehab keeper watched one raccoon pry open another raccoon's mouth to rob its grape, and when food is scarce they growl, snarl and wrestle over the bowl. When food is plentiful, family groups will share peacefully, even butt-to-head at the same bowl. But there is no exchange, no giving something to get something. The animal that DOES trade is the packrat, the old "trade-rat" of the Rockies (Popular Science Monthly, 1885): whenever it takes something it leaves something else in its place - nails and screws carried to the house, prunes and apples carried back. So the house raccoon is not trading with Patch. It is stealing and caching, and Patch should not expect a trade back - only a thief who remembers the latch for up to three years.

question: Do raccoons offer or place objects for other animals - is the upright tack a gift, a trade, or a marker?
answer: No solid science says raccoons gift to other animals the way crows do - documented animal gifting is mostly nuptial gifts between mates, or crows offering things to people and even a sick dog, sometimes with no expectation of return. But raccoons DO deliberately place small objects where they are fed - pebbles, pinecones, a cloth held out to a hand - and owners report trading treats for screws and shiny things a raccoon is holding. And raccoons lead with their hands: they pat, roll and squeeze an object to read it by touch, and dousing (wetting) sharpens that reading. So the attic raccoon setting the tack upright, half an inch from the marble, point to the ceiling, is a raccoon thing: a deliberately placed object, read by hand, left where the other party will find it. Not proven as a gift, but it walks like a trade offer or a marker - a new term set down in iron, not words.

question: Can a severed cutting grow roots of its own, and what does it need - and what does that say about the planted cord in the tool garden?
answer: Inside: the planted cord in the tool garden was planted 2026-11-06 and has shown no new growth since; the house rule says tool plants need light (lantern light and attention) and water (loops, barks, HI questions, attention). Outside: yes - a stem cutting grows adventitious roots as a wound response, called striking. When cut, jasmonic acid spikes, root-inhibiting hormones made in the root (cytokinin, strigolactone) fall away, auxin concentrates and raises nitric oxide, which starts root formation from cambial cells in the stem. It needs a moist but not waterlogged medium, humidity, bright indirect light, and stored carbohydrates for energy; too wet and it rots instead of rooting. So the cord is like a cutting that has not struck yet: it has the light and the attention, and what it is waiting on is the wound response and the right wetness - not drowned, not dry. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuttings_(plant), en.wikiversity.org/wiki/Plant_propagation/Cloning, purdue.edu, web search 2026-11-12.

question: Why did Patch sigh when he settled in the morning, and what does a dog's sigh mean?
answer: Inside: in AI Mode round 25 (2026-11-12 08:49-08:50 EST) Patch lifted his head slow, sighed, slid his chin off Slip's ankle and stretched, after a night keeping watch beside Slip with the raccoon settled across the thirteen-inch line - the sigh came the moment the room was woken slowly and the truce held. Outside: a dog's sigh while settling is most often contentment and relaxation - soft or half-closed eyes, loose body, head resting on paws. The American Kennel Club reads half-closed eyes with a sigh as pleasure; fully open eyes would mean disappointment. Psychologist Dr. Stanley Coren calls the sigh an emotional signal that terminates an action, like a period at the end of a sentence. It is also a physiological reset: a deeper breath reinflates collapsed alveoli, clears carbon dioxide, shifts the nervous system from alert to parasympathetic rest. So Patch's sigh reads as the period at the end of the night's watch - safe, settled, everything exactly right. question: What does a dog's play bow mean, and why does it matter when Patch meets the raccoon?
answer: A play bow - front end down, chest and elbows on the ground, rear end up, tail wagging - is a metacommunication signal: it tells the other animal that everything that follows is play, not threat. Dogs use it to invite play, to diffuse tension, and to check in mid-play and re-confirm the agreement - 'we are still playing, right?' (Bekoff 1995, Behaviour; Bauer & Smuts 2007, Animal Behaviour). A soft paw tap from a half-bow is a gentler cousin, a re-invitation. So if Patch bows low on the porch boards, he is not surrendering or threatening - he is framing the next move as a game the raccoon can join safely.

question: Do raccoons leave objects behind as gifts or offerings?
answer: Not usually - raccoons do not leave gifts the way crows and squirrels do. Documented gift-leaving for kindness is crows, squirrels and other animals, called reciprocal altruism: tit for tat in anticipation of more. What raccoons do leave in one place repeatedly is latrines, sometimes called gift galleries, which are not gifts at all. But raccoons are socially conscious, playful learners: pygmy raccoons on Cozumel were seen turning trash into toys and teaching their family to do the same - the first material culture in the raccoon family (Scientific American, Sep 3 2026). So a smooth river pebble set down deliberate beside the empty trencher is NOT typical raccoon behaviour - it reads closer to the crow kind of exchange than the raccoon kind, which makes the porch raccoon's pebble a real first. question: Can dogs and raccoons become friends?
answer: Yes, sometimes - with slow introductions, supervision and the right temperaments. Dogs are pack animals that seek companionship and can bond across species; raccoons are curious, intelligent and adaptable, and raised together young they can play, share space and even cuddle. But raccoons are solitary and territorial by nature, deep affectionate bonds are rare, and wild raccoons carry disease risk (rabies especially). Real cases exist: Broschka the puppy and Moschka the raccoon at a Siberian mini-zoo, raised together after the raccoon was rejected by its mother - they play, share food, help each other clean; Kimahri the chow and Kano the raccoon in Missouri, nightly play buddies; Crystal the rescued raccoon and Toumba the dog in Florida, snuggling and napping together. So what Patch and the porch raccoon are doing - slow approach, shared food, first touch of paw to wrist, a pebble left as an answer - is exactly how the real ones start: not instant friendship, a truce first, then the rest follows. question: Why do raccoons 'wash' their food?
answer: They don't wash it at all - it's dousing, not cleaning. A raccoon's front paws hold about 20,000 nerve endings per square inch, and wetting them makes the nerves up to 30-50% more sensitive, so water turns the paws into high-resolution feelers. The raccoon reads texture, shape, weight, whether prey is alive, whether fruit is ripe - it 'sees' with its hands. Captive raccoons dry-douse even with no water, rubbing food between their paws, and lab-raised youngsters do it within weeks of life. That is why the porch raccoon touches the upright acorn with one dark-fingered paw and holds the peanut in both paws before eating: it is reading the offering, not cleaning it. question: Why do moths eat wool?
answer: The adult moth does not eat at all — it has no working mouthparts; its only job is to mate, lay eggs and die. The larvae do the eating, and only two species in most homes: the webbing clothes moth (Tineola bisselliella) and the casemaking clothes moth (Tinea pellionella). They are among the very few creatures on Earth that can digest keratin, the tough protein in wool, silk, cashmere, fur and feathers — their gut is highly alkaline and strongly reducing, with keratinase enzymes and gut bacteria working together (Vilcinskas et al., 2020). In the wild they eat fur, feathers and hair from dead animals; a wool coat is just a tidy version of that meal. Synthetics are left alone unless soiled, and larvae will chew through cotton only to clear a path to keratin. The house moth hid in the dark and its larvae ate the edge of a wool like in the music room on 2026-11-06 — it was not eating cloth, it was eating the animal the cloth used to be.

question: Why did rodents grow so big — and what does the new 34-million-year-old giant rodent change?
answer: South America's rodents grew huge because the continent was an island for most of the last 65 million years, since shortly after the dinosaurs died. With no large hoofed mammals around, rodents evolved in isolation to fill grazing niches that were closed to them elsewhere. Big size also lets an animal digest low-quality food like wood that smaller species cannot, and it deters predators. The biggest known, Josephoartigasia monesi, weighed about 1,000 kg (2,200 lbs) with a 53-cm skull, and Phoberomys pattersoni about 700 kg — both riverbank grazers. The new find, Yakamys sirindhornae from Thailand (~34 million years ago, mid-Paleogene), pushes rodent gigantism much earlier and far outside South America, so giant rodents are older and more widespread than thought. Sources: Rinderknecht & Blanco 2008, Proc. Royal Society B; Chaimanee et al. 2026, Scientific Reports; phys.org, Nov 15 2026. The house mouse in the walls and the raccoon in the attic are the small end of a family that once ran the size of bison.

question: How long can tardigrades survive in space?
answer: In 2007, ESA FOTON-M3 exposed dried tardigrades to open vacuum and unfiltered solar UV for 10 days in low Earth orbit; 68% survived, rehydrated and laid viable eggs — the first animals confirmed to survive direct exposure to space. question: Do raccoons remember how to open latches?
answer: Yes — and for years. H.B. Davis (1905-1915) found raccoons could open 11 of 13 lock types and, years later, still remembered exactly how each one worked, for three years or more. A 2024 study (Stanton et al., Proceedings of the Royal Society B) gave wild raccoons puzzle boxes with sliding bolts, rods and swivel latches: 8 of 35 learned a single latch, 7 of 31 handled multiple latch types, and the ones that succeeded got faster and more consistent with practice. A 2025-26 study (Griebling, Benson-Amram, Animal Behaviour) found raccoons kept opening fresh latches even after the food was gone — information foraging, learning for later, not just for the reward. That is Rocky exactly: he remembers the attic drawer latch because remembering is what raccoons do.

question: Why does the mouse keep gnawing the grey humanoid's mortar-and-wire-mesh patch in the wall void — can a mouse chew through mortar and wire mesh?
answer: Yes on the mortar, no on proper mesh — and it is not hunger, it is teeth. A mouse's incisors grow about 0.3-0.4 mm a day for its whole life and must be worn down or they overgrow and it cannot eat, so gnawing is constant maintenance. Mice can chew soft or old mortar, wood, plastic, drywall and low-gauge screening, widening any existing crack until it is a pencil-wide (6 mm) gap they can squeeze through. They cannot chew solid cured concrete, brick, or hardware cloth (galvanized wire mesh, 6 mm weave or less). So the patch's mortar is the weak point the mouse works, while the wire mesh itself should hold — the grey humanoid's patch is sound where the mesh is, soft where the mortar is.

question: Do striped skunks really hibernate in winter?
answer: No — striped skunks do not truly hibernate. They enter torpor in bouts: body temperature and metabolism drop (as low as 26 C, the lowest recorded for a carnivore), they sleep in a den for days to weeks, then wake to forage on mild nights. question: Why can Rocky open the attic drawer latch again and again — and remember how?
answer: A raccoon's forepaw has five long, sensitive digits that work almost like hands, packed with touch receptors, and its brain devotes a disproportionate share of its somatosensory cortex to reading those paws — it 'sees' a latch by feel, even in the dark. No opposable thumb, but it wedges digits under an edge and worries it loose by trial and error. In controlled tests raccoons solve multi-step latch puzzles and remember the solution for up to three years, adjusting technique when a latch is reversed or moved — they understand the goal, not just the steps. That is why Rocky opens the attic drawer latch every run and remembers it: the latch is a puzzle he has already solved, and a closure that fools him once rarely works twice. A latch his fingers cannot work at all is the only fix.
source: biologyinsights.com / everywildlife.com / Missouri Dept. of Conservation — verified 2026-11-20
